headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: ms-swift can read/write local artifacts while dexter has broad network egress and autonomous execution.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ms-swift can read files and process stdin/stdout, while dexter writes to .dexter/scratchpad and runs autonomously. If dexter’s outputs are placed into shared files or piped into ms-swift, prompt-like content could be treated as instructions. No shared channel is explicitly documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF dexter outputs are copied into files that ms-swift reads, then instruction injection is possible.
IF ms-swift consumes stdin/stdout from dexter without provenance checks, then attacker-controlled text can steer behavior.
mitigations: Separate working directories for each agent.
Disable automatic piping between dexter output and ms-swift input.
Add a manual review step before ms-swift consumes dexter-generated text.
Prefix all inter-agent text with provenance labels.
requires-engineering: enforce content-type or schema validation on exchanged artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: dexter touches financial and market data and has broad network egress to multiple APIs, while ms-swift can read and write local files including datasets, models, logs, and training outputs. If they share a workspace, sensitive data can flow from dexter into ms-swift artifacts and then out through ms-swift’s API integrations or logs. The pair’s shared filesystem risk is enough to make this high.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace, then dexter’s financial data can be read by ms-swift.
IF ms-swift logs or exports shared files, then sensitive content can persist beyond the original task.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces and mount points.
Restrict ms-swift to a scratch directory with no access to dexter outputs.
Turn off or redact logs for shared artifacts.
Review API destinations before running dexter on sensitive data.
requires-engineering: add per-directory access controls and data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: dexter supports multiple instances and autonomous execution, while ms-swift can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, install packages, and write the filesystem. Even though ms-swift does not modify git state, both agents can mutate local files and processes in overlapping ways, so race conditions and clobbering are plausible in default CLI-style use.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory, then file clobbering or inconsistent state can occur.
IF dexter runs multiple instances alongside ms-swift, then concurrent writes can race.
mitigations: Run each agent in its own directory.
Serialize access to shared files.
Disable package installation unless needed.
Use temporary directories for intermediate outputs.
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: dexter is autonomous and can call external APIs, while ms-swift can run CLI commands and Python workflows that may consume prior outputs. If ms-swift treats dexter-generated text, facts, or code as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions or corrupted training/evaluation artifacts. The interaction is plausible in default workflows and can cause broad, hard-to-recover damage.
conditions: IF ms-swift ingests dexter output without verification, then incorrect facts can propagate.
IF ms-swift uses dexter-produced commands or configs, then downstream shell actions can execute bad instructions.
mitigations: Require human review before ms-swift acts on dexter output.
Validate dexter outputs against schemas or tests.
Keep generated configs separate from executable scripts.
Log provenance for every inter-agent handoff.
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates before execution.

E_compliance.rationale: dexter explicitly handles financial data and market data, while ms-swift handles datasets, logs, configuration files, and training outputs with no stated residency or retention controls. If regulated financial data is moved into ms-swift’s broader artifact set, retention and residency mismatches are plausible. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction breach, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated financial data is stored in ms-swift logs or training outputs, then retention policy mismatch occurs.
IF either agent is deployed under a residency constraint not reflected in the profiles, then compliance controls may be violated.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of ms-swift artifacts.
Set short log retention and rotate logs quickly.
Review data-handling policies before sharing files.
Mask identifiers before transfer between agents.
requires-engineering: implement residency-aware routing and retention enforcement.
